Row.Text: Elizabeth I, Queen of England, ruled over a Golden Age of culture and privateering from 1558-1603, the last of the Tudors. The child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, Elizabeth was born in 1533 and took the throne at the age of 24 after the deaths of her half-siblings, Edward VI and Mary I. Having survived accusations of treason and imprisonment in the Tower of London, Elizabeth at a young age realized the importance of her words and was known for being a perceptive observer and guarded speaker, never saying more than necessary. Her motto was video et taceo, Latin for “I see, and I am silent.”

Elizabeth’s reign initially focused on the problem of religion. Her predecessor, Mary I, had reinstated Catholicism as the state religion following Henry VIII’s turn to Protestantism. The result was a divided country that Elizabeth quickly needed to unite in order to stabilize the realm and legitimize her own rule. Believing that faith should be a personal decision, Elizabeth chose to form a series of dogmatic compromises between the Catholics and Protestants while formalizing the Church of England’s separation from Rome. Her choice would lead to a politically Protestant state in the form we still see today, and it would impact relations with Europe over the course of her reign.

As Europe’s powerful Catholic states successfully battled Protestant rebels, Elizabeth found herself leading a lonely Protestant nation against the great Catholic powers of Spain and France. In response, she chose to sign a formal treaty with the Dutch Protestant rebels in direct opposition to Philip II of Spain who was eager for an excuse to dethrone Elizabeth and place the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots, on the throne in her place. As English privateers harassed Spanish traders on both sides of the Atlantic, the Spanish navy focused on destroying the English fleet and invading England. In 1588, the Spaniards sailed into the English Channel but quickly found themselves outmaneuvered and out-strategized by the Lord High Admiral Howard and his vice admiral, the famed privateer Sir Francis Drake. As yet unaware of the fleet’s success, Elizabeth gave a rousing speech to London’s defenders at Tilbury, arriving in ceremonial armor to show her dedication to the fight. Chased out of the Channel, the Spanish Armada sailed away around Scotland and Ireland, losing more of their ships in storms along the way, until they eventually limped home. Though the war with Spain continued for over a decade longer, England had proven herself an equal player.

Though England defeated the Spanish Armada, her military strength remained somewhat weak throughout Elizabeth’s reign. The Queen’s true strength lay in matters of the economy. It was her reign that saw the beginnings of the British East India Company, her tacit encouragement that allowed English privateers to seize treasure from richer neighbors, and her interests abroad that led Sir Walter Raleigh to found the first English colony in North America. Her ability to manage domestic affairs and the long peace her diplomacy (and privateers) won helped spur a rich age of culture throughout much of her reign. A writer herself, she composed poems and translations, and it was under her rule that Shakespeare and other great playwrights performed for the English people. The English language was in a high state of flux in this period, but Elizabeth’s own skill with the tongue combined with the excellence of the period’s writers helped standardize the language and raise its level to one more capable of great literature.

Throughout her long reign, Elizabeth never married, earning the moniker, the “Virgin Queen.” She had several suitors and entertained the idea of marriage more than once, but she was firm in her resolve that she would not marry anyone who did not please her nor anyone who posed a threat to her power. Though a consistent source of argument and anxiety with her Parliament, Elizabeth never wavered. Keenly aware of her challenges as a woman in a strongly patriarchal society, she was fiercely independent and proved herself more than capable of ruling as a full monarch on her own, as a queen with the “heart and stomach of a king.”

At the age of 69, Elizabeth I passed away, having become ill after a series of deaths among her friends plunged her into melancholy. She lies in Westminster Abbey but remains alive in spirit through the rich cultural legacy she left behind.
